summary: Describes the Handover Keying (HOKEY) problem of re-authenticating quickly when a mobile device moves between access points. The existing EAP key framework forces a full EAP exchange again, which causes long delays. It states design goals for reusing derived keying material in handovers. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Showing your ticket again each time you walk into a new room is slow. This paper asks how to prove who you are once and move around quickly.

subtitle: Speeding up authentication when mobile devices move between access points

tldr.problem: When a mobile device moves between WiFi access points or cellular towers, it has to prove its identity to a new authenticator, but the standard EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) forces a full re-authentication that takes many round trips and unacceptable delay.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5169 defines design goals for HOKEY (Handover Key Management), a system to reuse cryptographic keys derived during initial authentication so that re-authentication at a new access point becomes a single fast round trip instead of multiple trips to the home server.
tldr.outcome: This problem statement sets the direction for fast handover protocols that allow mobile users to roam between networks without significant delay, preserving the 'always-on' experience for real-time applications like voice and video.

facts.label: Target domain
facts.value: Handover within a single administrative domain

today: RFC 5169 is a problem statement, not a protocol specification. It has guided the development of the HOKEY working group (now concluded), which produced solution RFCs including RFC 5296 (EAP Extensions) and RFC 5749 (HOKEY Protocol). The problem it addresses remains relevant to mobile network deployments, particularly as WiFi and cellular networks increasingly overlap.

sections.title: The Handover Authentication Problem
sections.content:
When a mobile device moves from one access point to another, it must authenticate to the new authenticator. Today this requires a full EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) exchange, which involves multiple round trips.

A typical EAP-TLS (one common method) takes at least 3 to 4 round trips. When the home EAP server is distant (across continents, with 100 to 300 milliseconds round-trip delay per leg), and each round trip also adds processing delay (milliseconds for fast crypto, hundreds for public-key operations), the total handover latency becomes unacceptable for real-time services like voice calls or video streams.

RFC 5169 documents this problem and sets design goals for a solution: HOKEY, which would let devices re-authenticate using keys already obtained during initial authentication.
sections.eli5: Checking your passport at every border takes minutes. What if you could show a faster proof after the first check?

sections.title: Key Concepts
sections.content:
The RFC defines the EAP architecture. The peer is the mobile device. The authenticator is the access point or base station. The EAP server is the backend server (often far away) that actually verifies credentials.

A third component, the AAA (Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting) server, acts as an intermediary: it encapsulates EAP messages in RADIUS or Diameter protocols and manages key distribution.

During authentication, both the peer and the server derive cryptographic keys, called the Master Session Key (MSK) and Extended Master Session Key (EMSK). The core idea of HOKEY is to use these keys to derive new keys for subsequent authenticators without re-running the expensive initial authentication.
sections.eli5: Think of the first authentication as proving your identity to a security guard. The guard gives you a magic ticket (the key). Later guards can verify the ticket without checking your passport again.

sections.title: Design Goals for Fast Re-Authentication
sections.content:
RFC 5169 lists the essential requirements for a HOKEY solution:

Lower latency: The protocol must reduce handover delay compared to a full EAP exchange. Method independence: It should work with any EAP method (SIM, AKA, TLS, etc.) without modifying them. Layer independence: It should work over any access technology (WiFi 802.11, WCDMA cellular, WiMAX, etc.).

Compatibility: Old devices that do not support fast re-authentication must still work in networks that support it, and vice versa. Cryptographic agility: The protocol must support algorithm negotiation so it can adapt as cryptography evolves.

The solution must also consider practical deployment: it should minimize changes needed to existing infrastructure and require minimal additional state at network devices.
sections.eli5: The solution must be fast, work with any authentication method, work everywhere, not break old devices, and not require replacing all the routers.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
Reusing old keys for new handovers creates new security risks. RFC 5169 outlines security goals based on RFC 4962 (AAA Key Management Guidance):

Key context and scope: Each key must have a clearly defined lifetime and context (what it is used for, where it can be used). Lower-level keys derived from a parent key must not outlive the parent. If one authenticator is compromised, its keys should not reveal keys at other authenticators.

Key freshness: The system must create cryptographically separate child keys from a parent key, and provide mechanisms to refresh keys regularly.

Authentication and authorization: Participants must prove their identity to one another, and the network must verify that each user is authorized to access each new authenticator. Channel binding: Intermediate authenticators must not be able to trick the peer or server into disagreeing about service terms.
sections.eli5: Using a cached key is faster but riskier. If a bad guy steals the ticket, he can forge another one. So the key must expire, you need multiple separate keys, and checks must prevent forgery.

sections.title: Related Work and Deployment
sections.content:
The RFC surveys existing fast re-authentication mechanisms. EAP-SIM and EAP-AKA already support fast re-authentication using symmetric-key crypto, requiring only one local round trip after the initial authentication. However, this still requires a round trip to the home EAP server.

IEEE 802.11r (WiFi fast roaming) handles handover between access points in the same network domain without EAP, using cached keys. But it does not allow roaming to a different operator's network.

CAPWAP (used in enterprise WiFi networks) allows a device to roam between wireless access points without re-authentication by having a central controller cache the keys. HOKEY would extend this to allow roaming between different controllers or operators.

The goal is a solution that works across administrative boundaries and network types, not just within a single operator's infrastructure.
sections.eli5: Some WiFi networks already roam fast, but only within one company. HOKEY would make it work between different companies too.
